candidate.answerReason: An equilateral triangle has one symmetry axis through each vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side, giving exactly three.

methods.label: Identify the three symmetry axes
methods.explanation: The lines containing the three altitudes of an equilateral triangle, which are also angle bisectors and medians, are all axes of symmetry. There are 3 in total.
methods.levelReason: Identifying symmetry axes and using the coincidence of altitude, median, and angle bisector are standard Grade 8 geometry.

candidate.annotationRationale:
The question assesses identifying and counting axes of symmetry, cnm_131. The written explanation also invokes the coincidence of altitudes, medians, and angle bisectors, covered by cnm_137 because an equilateral triangle is isosceles at every vertex. The altitude concept cnm_112 supports the stated description. A second proof would unnecessarily expand this familiar fact question.

candidate.changeReason: The three vertex-to-opposite-midpoint lines are precisely the symmetry axes of an equilateral triangle. The current explanation correctly identifies them and gives the count.

review.mathematicalCheck: Each vertex-to-opposite-midpoint line reflects the equilateral triangle onto itself. Any reflection symmetry must fix a vertex and interchange the other two, so these three distinct lines exhaust the axes. The retained factual explanation gives the correct count of 3.
review.levelCheck: Symmetry axes and the coincidence of medians, altitudes, and angle bisectors fit Grade 8.
review.methodDistinctness: One identification method is enough for this familiar fact question.
review.annotationCheck: cnm_131 matches the assessed symmetry count. cnm_137 legitimately applies at every vertex because an equilateral triangle is isosceles relative to each chosen base; cnm_112 supports the altitude terminology.
